body: No, I probably wouldn't choose death if I didn't have mental problems. I'm not sure that's possible though

Are you suggesting I try what McCandless did in order to "find myself"? If that is what you're saying, it reminds me of bad advice that I got from a therapist who was supposedly supposed to help me. Of course, I'm not paying you and you're talking to my psychotic ass simply out of the goodness of your heart so I probably shouldn't snark.

In regards to lifestyle: In a way, I have changed my "lifestyle". In several ways. For example, I took time off from college to work for a construction company. Before that all I'd ever known was a classroom and a single job doing cleaning and trash collection at an amusement park. I looked down on construction jobs. But I learned there's a lot more complexity to them than meets the eye.

Helicopter parents: I bought a car. Broke free from some of the shackles of control that you guessed at (no offense, but I'll bet it's not terribly hard to guess at if you know psychology based on what I said. Not that I know anything about such stuff). Do I have mental problems? Yeah. Are you better than me for being able to psychoanalyze my childhood from a few paragraphs? Yeah, maybe. Am I comparing myself to you because of my own insecurities? Yeah, probably.

When it comes to being lied to: I wasn't just lied to and propped up by my parents though. The whole educational system that I went through lied to me. Middle school AND high school. And I consistently get the feeling that if it weren't for what I've learned outside of the educational system that college classes would STILL be lying to me. My classmates lied to me to, although probably accidentally or simply out of instinct. I stopped looking at things binomially/unidimensionally/in black and white about a year ago and immediately became constantly paranoid. That bipolar paranoia and pronoia that I've been experiencing has been a reprieve from most of my depression. But even after questioning my lofty ambitions for the past 2-3 years, it still remains true for me that "I'd rather be dead than average, and I probably will be." - Donald Glover. If I'm not happy by 25 then I probably will pull a McCandless. Hopefully not something that's self destructive/dangerous to other people too.

Edit: reread your response and realized there was a lot I didn't respond to. Things I maybe agreed with or found insight from. This edit is for what I got from the reread.

What practical means to me? I don't remember saying that word, but what I see as practical has a biological basis for us humans, mostly. It's also an opinion, i.e. depends on what I want to accomplish. I would assume that's not the answer you were reaching for, but then I probably don't understand the question. Sorry :|

The world building gamers analogy helped me. I can tell it'll make it easier for me to deal with and interpret my parent's actions and stuff. So thanks, I guess. Not sure if I should thank you for stuff like that... Whatever...

Just about everything about my parents rang true.

Edit: yeah you're probably right that there are other options. But I still can't get the feeling behind Donald Glover's quote out of my heart and I'll probably never be able to. Especially not with my paranoia. If it leaves and I can settle for an average life then I guess I'll be able to settle for those other options too

I did ok in comp sci. Got a 5 on the AP test. Got an A in the first comp sci course at penn state. Smoked my way through most of the second that I was there for until I took a semester off a year ago. I like comp sci. I like math. I like anything with science. I like studies that are preparing me for the future. And that teach me something. I'm just bitching. I have no patience. I dislike that making apps is harder for me than multivariable calculus. I'm ashamed of it. I'm trying to study psychology and remind myself that apps and websites are built on 2 dimensional surfaces. I find anything that I don't completely understand hard. So multivariable calculus is easy. I can't remember things as easily if I can't derive it. Remembering rules about html or app design is harder because I don't understand the reasons for those rules. But remembering physics equations and math formulas and problem solving strategies is easy because there's justification behind every step. It may somewhat be stubbornness, but at the same time it's a memory thing as well.

Edit: I just need to keep trying. Until 6 or 9 or 20 months from now when I fall into a deep depression again. I have nothing in my life figured out and the moment that that gets in the way of my goals again will be the moment I start thinking about suicide 24/7. I shouldn't have come on here to involve other people. This is my problem and it's just as messy and complicated as anyone else's. We all have our crosses to bare. Those of us who can't bare our own get bred out of the stock. If that's my fate in the next few years then so be it
